scenarios.title: January 2008: the first crack after the record high
scenarios.briefing: Mid-January 2008. The Sensex set an intraday record of 21,206.77 on January 10, 2008, after a powerful multi-year bull run, and has slipped back since. Global markets are nervous about the health of the US economy and its housing and credit markets. Domestic sentiment, IPO activity and leverage in the market are all high. You hold cash and can trade large caps across banks, energy, infrastructure, real estate and IT.
scenarios.debrief: On Monday, January 21, 2008 the Sensex fell 1,408.35 points (7.41%) to close at 17,605.35, then its biggest single-day point fall, amid FII selling, margin calls and US recession fears. On January 22 the market opened sharply lower and breached the 10% index circuit breaker: NSE closed its capital market segment at 9:55:58 for one hour and trading resumed at 10:55. The Sensex hit an intraday low of 15,332.42 before recovering to close 875.41 points lower; the Nifty closed at 4,899.30, down 309.50 points (5.94%). Later that day (US time) the Federal Reserve made an unscheduled 75 bp cut to 3.5%. The January 10 intraday high was not surpassed until November 2013.

Sensex closes down 1,408.35 points (7.41%) at 17,605.35, its biggest single-day point fall to that date.

US Federal Reserve makes an unscheduled 75 bp cut in the fed funds target to 3.5%.

learning_goals: Experience a gap-down through a market-wide circuit breaker and see that stop orders cannot fill while trading is halted
Recognise how leverage and margin calls amplify a fall
Decide whether to buy a sharp one-day rebound or treat it as a bear-market rally

scenarios.title: Autumn 2008: Lehman, liquidity and emergency rate cuts
scenarios.briefing: Mid-September 2008. The Sensex is far below its January 2008 record after a year of falls. The US financial system has been under stress for months and investors are watching large US financial institutions closely. The RBI has been fighting inflation with tight policy (repo at 9%, CRR at 9%). Banks, infrastructure and real estate names have been hit hardest so far; FMCG and some defensives have held up better.
scenarios.debrief: Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on September 15, 2008; the Sensex closed 469.54 points lower at 13,531.27 that day after falling over 800 points intraday. Through October the RBI shifted to emergency easing: a 50 bp CRR cut announced on Monday October 6, a further cut announced October 10 that took CRR to 7.5% from 9% (the Sensex closed down 792 points at 10,537 that day), and a 100 bp repo cut to 8.0% effective October 20. On October 24, after the RBI's mid-term policy review disappointed and global markets fell, the Sensex dropped 1,070 points (about 11%) to close at 8,701, below 9,000. The Sensex lost about 24% in October alone.

timeline.event: Lehman Brothers bankruptcy; Sensex closes down 469.54 points at 13,531.27 after an intraday fall of over 800 points.

learning_goals: See that the first policy response does not necessarily mark the bottom
Practise sizing positions when daily volatility is several times normal
Compare drawdowns in high-beta sectors (banks, real estate, capital goods) with defensives

scenarios.title: May 2009: the election result nobody priced in
scenarios.briefing: Friday, May 15, 2009. India's month-long general election is over and votes will be counted on Saturday, May 16; markets reopen Monday. Exit polls point to neither the Congress-led UPA nor the BJP-led NDA reaching a majority on its own, and the widely held view is a hung parliament that would need coalition bargaining. Markets have been recovering from the 2008 crash. Decide what exposure you want to carry over the weekend.
scenarios.debrief: The UPA won about 262 seats, far above the roughly 195 the exit polls had suggested and only about 10 short of a majority, so it could govern without depending on the Left. On Monday, May 18, 2009, the Sensex and Nifty hit an upper circuit within seconds of the open; equity and derivatives trading was halted for two hours, and on reopening the indices hit the next upper circuit and trading was closed for the day. These were the first upper-circuit halts in the market's history; short covering amplified the move.

timeline.event: Lok Sabha results announced; UPA wins about 262 seats versus exit-poll estimates of about 195.
Indices hit an upper circuit at the open; equity and equity-derivatives markets closed for two hours.
Second upper circuit on reopening; trading closed for the rest of the day.

learning_goals: Understand event risk held over a weekend: a binary outcome can gap prices beyond any order level
See that a short position can be impossible to exit when the market is locked at an upper circuit
Distinguish consensus expectations (exit polls) from outcomes

scenarios.title: 2013 taper tantrum: when the Fed talks, the rupee walks
scenarios.briefing: May 21, 2013. The US Federal Reserve is buying $85 billion of bonds a month and global liquidity has supported emerging markets. India runs a wide current-account deficit and inflation is elevated. Foreign investors have been active buyers of Indian debt and equities. The rupee and India's import-heavy and rate-sensitive sectors are sensitive to any change in global capital flows.
scenarios.debrief: On May 22, 2013 Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke first signalled the Fed could pare its bond buying. Foreign funds pulled about $12 billion from Indian debt and equities over the following three months and the rupee fell to a record intraday low of 68.85 per dollar on August 28, 2013; the RBI sold dollars to slow the slide. Raghuram Rajan took charge as RBI Governor on September 4 and announced a set of measures; the Sensex rose about 333 points that day as the rupee recovered. On September 18 (US time) the Fed unexpectedly kept its purchases unchanged, and on September 19 the Sensex jumped 684.48 points (3.43%) to 20,646.64. On September 20 Rajan raised the repo rate for the first time in nearly two years, and the market gave back some gains.

learning_goals: Link a currency shock to sector winners (IT exporters) and losers (importers, rate-sensitive banks)
See how foreign capital flows drive Indian markets independently of domestic earnings
Handle policy-surprise days in both directions

scenarios.title: November 2016: demonetisation night (and a US election)
scenarios.briefing: Close of trading, Tuesday, November 8, 2016. Indian markets have had a steady year. Voting in the US presidential election is under way and results will arrive during Indian market hours tomorrow. You hold cash and can trade banks, real estate, consumer and auto names.
scenarios.debrief: On the evening of November 8, 2016 the government announced that Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 notes would cease to be legal tender from midnight; old notes could be deposited in bank accounts from November 10 until December 30, 2016. On November 9, with Donald Trump also leading the US election count, the Sensex fell about 1,689 points (around 6%) intraday, its worst intraday plunge in nearly 15 months, but recovered to close down 338.61 points (1.23%) at 27,252.53; real estate was among the worst hit. In the fortnight after the announcement the Sensex fell 6.6%. Worries about the cash crunch's effect on growth persisted (factory activity slowed sharply in November), and by December 22 the Sensex had erased its 2016 year-to-date gains.

Sensex falls about 1,689 points intraday on demonetisation and Trump's lead.

learning_goals: Separate two simultaneous shocks (domestic policy and a global event) when explaining a move
See how a scary open can reverse intraday, and why panic market orders at the open are costly
Identify which sectors depend on cash transactions

scenarios.title: September 2018: IL&FS defaults and the NBFC liquidity scare
scenarios.briefing: Friday, September 14, 2018. Infrastructure lender IL&FS, a large and highly rated borrower in the money markets, has been struggling to meet short-term obligations, and its credit ratings have already been cut to sub-investment grade. Non-bank lenders (NBFCs and housing finance companies) have grown fast by funding themselves through commercial paper bought largely by mutual funds. Their stocks have been market favourites.
scenarios.debrief: IL&FS could not meet commercial-paper redemptions due September 14, 2018, and on Monday September 17 ICRA cut its ratings to default grade ('D'). Fear spread to other wholesale-funded lenders. On Friday September 21, after a mutual fund sold DHFL commercial paper at a higher yield, DHFL fell as much as 59.67% intraday to Rs 246.25 and closed 42.43% lower at Rs 351.55 on BSE; other housing finance companies also crashed. The same morning YES Bank fell 34% after the RBI declined to extend CEO Rana Kapoor's term beyond January 31, 2019. DHFL said it had not defaulted and had no IL&FS exposure; it rebounded about 25% intraday on September 24 after CARE and ICRA reaffirmed its ratings. On October 1, the NCLT allowed the government to supersede the IL&FS board and install a new board led by Uday Kotak.

learning_goals: Understand funding-liquidity risk: lenders that borrow short and lend long are exposed when credit markets freeze
See contagion from one issuer to a whole sector
Practise not averaging down on a stock in a liquidity panic without a clear thesis

scenarios.title: October 2019: a whistleblower letter hits an IT bellwether
scenarios.briefing: Friday, October 18, 2019. Infosys reported its September-quarter results earlier this month and is one of India's most widely held large caps. IT services stocks are seen as defensive, steady compounders. You can trade Infosys and its large IT peers.
scenarios.debrief: On October 21, 2019 a whistleblower complaint by a group calling itself 'Ethical Employees' became public, alleging CEO Salil Parekh and CFO Nilanjan Roy pushed unethical practices to inflate short-term revenue and profit. Infosys said the complaint had been placed before the audit committee and an independent investigation by Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas was under way. On October 22 Infosys shares closed down 16.21% at Rs 643.30 on BSE, wiping about Rs 53,451 crore of market value, the sharpest intraday fall in over six years. On October 24 the stock fell about 2% more after the company disclosed the US SEC had begun an investigation. On January 10, 2020 the audit committee said it found no evidence of financial impropriety or executive misconduct and no restatement was warranted.

learning_goals: See single-stock gap risk in a 'safe' large cap and why diversification matters

scenarios.title: February–March 2020: the COVID crash
scenarios.briefing: Thursday, February 20, 2020. The Nifty is not far from its January record high. A new coronavirus outbreak that began in China has disrupted Chinese factories and travel, and cases are being reported in other countries; India has very few reported cases. Markets have so far treated it mainly as a China supply-chain issue. Your universe spans banks, IT, consumer, auto, aviation and pharma.
scenarios.debrief: The sell-off accelerated as the virus spread globally. After the WHO called the outbreak a pandemic late on March 11, the Sensex fell 2,919.26 points (8.18%) to 32,778.14 on March 12. Market-wide circuit breakers were hit on two days: on March 13 the Nifty hit its 10% lower circuit in early trade and trading was halted for 45 minutes, after which the market recovered sharply; on March 23, as states announced lockdowns, the Sensex hit its 10% lower circuit at 9:58 am, trading was halted for 45 minutes, and it closed down 3,934.72 points (13.15%) at 25,981.24, its biggest one-day fall. The Nifty closed at its low of the episode on March 23 (about 7,610) and made its intraday low of 7,511 on March 24, about 40% below its record high. That evening the Prime Minister announced a 21-day nationwide lockdown, and on March 27 the RBI cut the repo rate by 75 bp to 4.40% and permitted a three-month moratorium on term-loan instalments. The Nifty was back above 8,000 within two sessions of the low.

scenarios.title: March 2020: Yes Bank is placed under moratorium
scenarios.briefing: Wednesday, March 4, 2020. Yes Bank, once one of India's fastest-growing private lenders, has spent much of the last two years dealing with regulatory action, a leadership change and asset-quality problems, and has been trying to raise fresh capital. Its share price has already fallen a long way. Global markets are also volatile because of the coronavirus outbreak.
scenarios.debrief: On the evening of March 5, 2020 the government, on the RBI's application, placed Yes Bank under a 30-day moratorium, capped depositor withdrawals at Rs 50,000, and the RBI superseded its board, appointing former SBI CFO Prashant Kumar as administrator. On March 6 the stock fell as much as 84.93% to Rs 5.55 intraday and closed down 56.04% at Rs 16.20; SBI fell 6.19%, IndusInd 5.62% and ICICI Bank 3.67%, and the Sensex closed 893.99 points lower. A draft reconstruction scheme had SBI taking up to a 49% stake. The government notified the Yes Bank reconstruction scheme effective March 13, with SBI holding at least 26% for three years and a three-year lock-in on 75% of holdings for other shareholders with 100 or more shares; the moratorium was lifted at 6 pm on March 18, 2020. All of this unfolded alongside the COVID market crash.

learning_goals: See how a regulatory action can wipe out most of a stock's value overnight
Understand lock-in clauses: a rescue can protect depositors without protecting shareholders' liquidity
Separate stock-specific risk from sector contagion

scenarios.title: April 2020 – February 2021: the recovery rally
scenarios.briefing: Tuesday, March 31, 2020. India entered a 21-day nationwide lockdown on March 25 and the economic damage is unknown. The Sensex and Nifty suffered their worst falls in history in March. The RBI has cut the repo rate to 4.40% and allowed a three-month moratorium on loan repayments. Central banks worldwide are easing aggressively. Earnings forecasts are being cut across sectors.
scenarios.debrief: Despite a deep economic contraction, equities recovered quickly. On May 22, 2020 the RBI cut the repo rate a further 40 bp to 4%, extended the loan moratorium by three months and said GDP would contract in FY21; the Sensex fell 260 points that day, led by banks. The Sensex reached 40,000 on October 8, 2020. After Pfizer–BioNTech's vaccine efficacy announcement on November 9, the Sensex crossed 43,000 for the first time on November 10. On January 21, 2021 it touched 50,000 for the first time (closing lower), having gone from 40,000 to 50,000 in 74 sessions and about 96% above its March 24, 2020 low. On February 1, 2021 the Union Budget sparked a 2,314.84-point (5%) Sensex gain, the best Budget-day gain since 1997.

scenarios.title: February–March 2022: war in Ukraine and an oil spike
scenarios.briefing: Tuesday, February 22, 2022. On February 21 Russian President Vladimir Putin recognised two breakaway regions in Ukraine's Donbas, sharply escalating tensions with Ukraine and the West. Crude oil prices have been rising. India imports most of its oil, so crude is a key variable for inflation, the rupee, oil marketing companies, airlines and paint makers. Upstream producers and metal companies may react differently.
scenarios.debrief: On February 24, 2022 Russia launched a wider military campaign in Ukraine. Oil rose above $100 a barrel for the first time since 2014 and the Sensex fell 2,702.15 points (4.72%) to 54,529.91, its biggest fall in two years; the Nifty lost 815 points to 16,247. Oil kept rising: Brent neared $120 by March 3, and on March 7 Brent touched about $139 intraday, its highest since 2008, on talk of a ban on Russian oil. That day the Sensex fell 1,491 points to an eight-month low of 52,842 and the rupee hit a record low of 77.20 per dollar.

scenarios.title: January 2023: a short-seller report and a pulled FPO
scenarios.briefing: Monday, January 23, 2023. The Adani group's listed companies have been among the market's best performers over the past few years and carry very high valuations. Adani Enterprises is preparing a Rs 20,000-crore follow-on public offer (FPO), one of India's largest. You can trade group companies, recently acquired cement makers, and large lenders and insurers with exposure to the group.
scenarios.debrief: On January 24, 2023 US short seller Hindenburg Research published a report alleging stock manipulation and accounting fraud at the Adani group, flagging high leverage, and disclosing a short position. The group called it 'maliciously mischievous' and baseless. Group stocks fell sharply in the following sessions (an $86 billion rout per Reuters). The FPO was fully subscribed on its last day, but on February 1 Adani Enterprises withdrew it, saying proceeding would not be 'morally correct', and promised refunds; many group stocks closed at lower circuits, and on February 2 several again hit 10% lower circuits early, with Adani Enterprises down 35% in two days and about Rs 8.7 lakh crore of group market value lost in six sessions. On March 2, GQG Partners bought Rs 15,446 crore of shares in Adani Enterprises, Adani Ports, Adani Green and Adani Transmission from the promoters in block deals, and group stocks rallied.

learning_goals: Experience concentration risk when a whole business group re-rates at once

scenarios.title: June 2024: exit-poll euphoria, result-day shock, fast recovery
scenarios.briefing: Friday, May 31, 2024. India's general election is in its final phase; exit polls will be released after voting ends and votes will be counted on Tuesday, June 4. The market broadly expects the BJP-led NDA to return with a large majority, and government-owned companies (PSUs), defence and infrastructure stocks have been strong performers on that view.
scenarios.debrief: On Monday, June 3, after exit polls predicted a landslide for the BJP-led NDA, the Sensex jumped 2,507.47 points (3.39%) to a record close of 76,468.78 and the Nifty closed at 23,263.90. On June 4 counting showed the BJP well short of a majority on its own (about 241 seats) with the NDA at about 294; the Sensex fell over 6,000 points intraday and closed down 4,390 points (5.74%) at about 72,079, the Nifty down 5.93% at 21,885, the largest one-day fall since 2020, with PSU stocks hit hard. Markets recovered quickly as NDA allies backed Narendra Modi for a third term; on June 7, after the RBI held rates and raised its FY25 growth forecast to 7.2%, the Sensex closed at a record 76,693.36.

timeline.event: First session after exit polls: Sensex up 2,507.47 points (3.39%) to a record 76,468.78.
Counting day: BJP short of majority alone; Sensex closes down 4,390 points (5.74%); Nifty down 5.93%.
RBI holds repo, raises FY25 GDP forecast to 7.2%; Sensex closes at a record 76,693.36.

learning_goals: See that consensus positioning raises the cost of being wrong on event day
Practise sizing into a binary event and planning exits before the result
Avoid panic selling at the bottom of a sentiment shock

scenarios.title: September 2024 – February 2025: record highs, then a five-month slide
scenarios.briefing: Friday, September 20, 2024. Indian equities are at record highs: on September 18 the US Federal Reserve cut rates by 50 bp, its first cut in over four years, and on September 19 the Sensex hit a record intraday high. Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have been buying, while domestic mutual-fund SIP flows remain strong. Indian valuations are high relative to other emerging markets.
scenarios.debrief: On September 24 China announced broad stimulus including rate and reserve-ratio cuts, and Chinese stocks rallied. The Nifty set an intraday record of 26,277 on September 27, 2024 (not surpassed until November 2025). FPIs then pulled a record of roughly Rs 94,000 crore from Indian equities in October 2024, citing high valuations, slowing earnings growth and cheaper Chinese stocks; domestic investors absorbed much of the selling. Outflows continued into 2025: about Rs 78,027 crore in January and more in February, taking 2025 outflows above Rs 1 lakh crore by late February amid US tariff worries, higher US bond yields and a strong dollar. The Nifty fell 12.65% from end-September to February 27 and was set for five consecutive monthly declines, its longest losing streak since 1996.

timeline.event: US Fed cuts rates by 50 bp to 4.75–5.00% (context; Sensex record intraday high on Sep 19).
China announces broad stimulus, including a 50 bp reserve-ratio cut.
Nifty intraday all-time high of 26,277.
October ends with record FPI equity outflow of about Rs 94,000 crore.
FPI outflows in 2025 cross Rs 1 lakh crore (Rs 78,027 crore in January alone).
Nifty down 12.65% from end-September; on track for a fifth straight monthly fall, first in 29 years.

learning_goals: Recognise a slow, grinding drawdown driven by flows rather than a single shock
Practise trailing stops and rebalancing near record highs
Understand how foreign and domestic flows can offset each other
